newsitem.title: GREECE: Three sailors charged with murder of immigrants.
newsitem.headline: Three sailors charged with murder of immigrants.

text.p: Three fugitive Greek sailors have been charged with mass murder in connection with allegations that some 280 illegal immigrants drowned in transit off the coast of Sicily last month, court officials said on Thursday.
"Three people have been charged with mass murder," the state prosecutor in the port town of Nafplion, Yannis Provataris, told Reuters.
"Only Greeks have been charged with murder because, according to international law, we can't charge foreigners for crimes committed outside Greece," he said.

Provataris charged eight other people, including foreigners, with illegal movement of immigrants in Greece and said testimony by the survivors "led to the conclusion there was a collision, a shipwreck, and that many people drowned."
He said an investigating magistrate could bring new charges if fresh evidence emerged during his inquiries.

Provataris based his charges largely on testimony by members of a group of more than 100 immigrants from India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka who were landed illegally in Greece on December 30. Many have since been arrested.
Those immigrants have said nearly 300 fellow travellers on board the Honduran-flagged Yioham were forced to transfer to a smaller ship in the Malta-Sicily channel on Christmas Day.
The smaller ship, believed to have been stolen from Malta, was then in collision with the Yioham while manoeuvering and sank, the immigrants said. Only 29 people were rescued.
Those charged with murder were Eftihios Zervoudakis, a sailor and among the rescued, Mihalis Fanourakis and Antonis Sfakianakis, both mechanics on the Yioham. All three are still at liberty.
Among those sought by police are Youssef Al Halal, the Yioham's captain and a Lebanese resident of Athens, Marcel Barbara, a Pakistani who reportedly lives in Malta and two Indians.
Pakistan's ambassador to Greece Rasheed Ahmad told Reuters he believed the chilling accounts of the ordeal given by the immigrants, even though no sign of the shipwreck had been found.

"I believe we are facing a big human tragedy," Ahmad said. "We talked with the Pakistanis arrested and their account is so detailed that we believe them. They would tell us the truth. They would not lie to us."
He added: "We had testimonies from people directly involved in this tragedy. One of the survivors saw his brother drown."
The embassy has compiled a report on the shipwreck with the names of 31 Pakistanis who were described as "deceased." Another list includes 37 Pakistanis held in Nafplion and nearby towns.
The report was published in the Pakistani press and worried relatives and friends have been calling the embassy, he said.
"The immigrants are mostly boys from villages back home. Farmers, who were not starving in Pakistan but wanted a better life and more money in Europe," Ahmad said.
He said Karachi authorities were trying to find the agents who arranged the illegal trip to Europe. The immigrants would be returned to Pakistan once the Greek investigation was over.

The Yioham continued its voyage after the collision and landed its cargo of illegal immigrants south of Nafplion on the Peloponnese coast. About 115 immigrants have been arrested and about 60 are thought to be still at large.

A Greek government statement last week said immigrants from Sri Lanka had paid $8,000 each in Colombo for an air ticket to Cairo and the sea trip to Europe. The Indians and Pakistanis said they paid $5,000 each, it said.
